explanations: luna: The rebuke of commanding righteousness while forgetting oneself offers a concrete form of self-preference that contrasts with giving another priority, though it is not about the Hereafter explicitly.
terra: Israel's exchange asks, أَتَسْتَبْدِلُونَ ٱلَّذِى هُوَ أَدْنَىٰ بِٱلَّذِى هُوَ خَيْرٌ, staging the section's condemned choice of the lower for the better.

luna: This ayah names humiliation in worldly life and severe punishment in the Hereafter as the consequence of breaking the covenant; the next ayah describes that conduct as buying worldly life for the Hereafter.

luna: The ayah condemns those who bought the life of this world at the price of the Hereafter, a concrete exchange of the better enduring outcome for the nearer one. | terra: Those who bought worldly life at the price of the hereafter turn preference into an exchange whose consequence cannot be reduced or relieved.
terra: A life of a thousand years would still not remove the covetous person from punishment, exposing mere longevity as counterfeit permanence.
terra: Whatever good people send ahead for themselves will be found with God, so present goods are retained by being transferred toward Him.
terra: God chose Abraham in the world and places him among the righteous in the hereafter, joining divine selection across the two lives.

luna: The ayah defines righteousness partly as giving wealth, despite love of it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, and others; this is a specific choice to direct possessions away from self. | terra: Giving cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, needy people, travelers, petitioners, and captives concretely enacts preferring needy others over possession.

luna: Here خير means property or an estate left behind, unlike “better” in the source section; that material sense matters because the section is weighing worldly property against enduring good. | terra: إِن تَرَكَ خَيْرًا uses “good” for property left behind, exemplifying the section's secondary wealth sense and combining it with what remains at death.

luna: Some ask only for good in worldly life and have no share in the Hereafter; this is the section’s condemned narrowing of what counts as a desirable outcome. | terra: The person whose prayer asks only for this world is said to have no share in the hereafter, one side of a paired choice.

luna: The neighboring supplication asks for good in both worlds and protection from the Fire, giving a balanced alternative to seeking only worldly good. | terra: The answering prayer seeks good in both world and hereafter, setting a right ordering that does not call every worldly good refuse.

luna: The next ayah says these people have a share from what they earned, completing the consequence of the balanced supplication. | terra: أُولَٰٓئِكَ لَهُمْ نَصِيبٌ مِّمَّا كَسَبُوا assigns the correctly ordered seekers a lasting earned portion and completes the pair.
luna: A person gives up the self in seeking God’s approval, a specific reversal of keeping worldly benefit for oneself.
terra: Worldly life is adorned for unbelievers who mock believers, but the God-fearing will be above them on resurrection day, reversing apparent rank.

luna: The ayah uses خير for property one can spend and directs that spending toward relatives, orphans, and the needy, connecting the source section’s material sense of “good” to how possessions are put to good use.
terra: People may dislike what is good for them and love what is bad for them; divine knowledge therefore corrects desire as a sufficient rule of selection.
terra: A believing slave is better than an admired polytheist, correcting a chooser who confuses social station or attraction with worth.
terra: Israel rejects Saul for lacking abundant wealth, but their prophet says God selected him and increased him in knowledge and stature, overturning their worldly criterion of worth.
terra: The Ark bears بَقِيَّةٌ of what the houses of Moses and Aaron left; this sacred remainder carries tranquility and serves as the sign of the chosen king.
terra: Charity ruined by reproach and display becomes dust on a smooth rock swept bare by rain, a deed chosen for appearance turning into residue with no yield.
terra: Sincere spending is a high garden whose rain multiplies its produce, the fruitful counterpart to 2:264's stripped rock.

luna: The source section’s account of خير as good that is not refuse connects to the command not to choose the inferior for charity—something the giver would accept only with eyes closed. | terra: Givers are told to spend wholesome earnings and not deliberately select the bad portion they themselves would accept only with closed eyes.
terra: Wisdom is called خَيْرًا كَثِيرًا, pairing goodness with abundance while locating that abundance in discernment rather than property.
terra: God makes usury waste away and causes charities to grow, distinguishing wealth that looks productive from clean giving that truly increases.

luna: The ayah stages the attractions of women, children, wealth, horses, cattle, and tilled land as worldly adornment; the next ayah offers what is better, making the object of preference concrete. | terra: Loved appetites, accumulated wealth, livestock, and tilled land are gathered as the enjoyment of worldly life, making the attractive lower pan concrete.

luna: After worldly desires are listed in the preceding ayah, this one offers something better: gardens, purified spouses, and God’s approval. It makes the section’s “better” concrete without treating worldly adornment as the final good. | terra: قُلْ أَؤُنَبِّئُكُم بِخَيْرٍ مِّن ذَٰلِكُمْ answers the worldly list with gardens, purified spouses, and God's approval, explicitly offering the better selection.
terra: God's selection of Adam, Noah, and Abraham's and Imran's houses over the worlds supplies a direct scene of the chooser and the chosen.

luna: One cannot reach righteousness until giving from what one loves; this makes the section’s contrast between self-reservation and a rightly directed preference concrete. | terra: People do not attain true goodness until they spend from what they love, making correct preference cost the surrender of a favored possession.
terra: The expenditure of rejecters is compared to a freezing wind that destroys a crop, another field image in which apparent stored value becomes loss.

luna: The ayah distinguishes those seeking the reward of this world from those seeking the reward of the Hereafter, while allowing that the first may receive some worldly return. | terra: The ayah places the seeker of worldly reward and the seeker of otherworldly reward in parallel clauses, making the selection and its apportioned result explicit.

luna: After the battle turns, the ayah distinguishes among those who desire the worldly gain and those who desire the Hereafter; it directly stages the two choices the section weighs. | terra: مِنكُم مَّن يُرِيدُ ٱلدُّنْيَا وَمِنكُم مَّن يُرِيدُ ٱلْءَاخِرَةَ identifies the battlefield split as two differently chosen ends.

luna: God will distinguish the impure from the pure; this supplies a sorting image for the section’s selected, refuse-free side, though the ayah’s main subject is testing believers. | terra: God does not leave the community mixed until He distinguishes the foul from the wholesome, directly staging the section's separation of select from refuse.

luna: Every soul will taste death and worldly life is only delusive enjoyment; success is entering the Garden, grounding the section’s question of what truly counts as winning. | terra: Full recompense comes at resurrection, worldly life is only deceptive enjoyment, and true success is defined by removal from Fire and entry into the Garden.
terra: The Prophet is told not to be deceived by unbelievers' free movement through the lands, introducing the apparent worldly advantage corrected in 3:197-198.
terra: That movement is only a little enjoyment followed by hell, supplying the passing side before 3:198 names what is better with God.
terra: After the warning not to be deceived by unbelievers' brief movement through the land, the ayah says what is with God is better for the righteous.
terra: وَلَا تَتَبَدَّلُوا۟ ٱلْخَبِيثَ بِٱلطَّيِّبِ forbids exchanging an orphan's sound property for bad property, a concrete wrongful sorting of wealth.

luna: Those who trade worldly life for the Hereafter are promised a great reward whether they are killed or victorious, giving the section’s preference a concrete faithful form. | terra: Those who sell worldly life for the hereafter are summoned to fight, making the rightly directed exchange the inverse of buying this life at the next life's expense.

luna: The ayah names worldly enjoyment as little and says the Hereafter is better for the mindful, an explicit valuation of the two sides in the section. | terra: The answer to people clinging to worldly delay says its enjoyment is little and the hereafter is better for the God-fearing.
terra: The warning against seeking the fleeting goods of worldly life adds that abundant gains are with God, correcting both the object and measure of the choice.

luna: The ayah asks who desires the reward of this world, then says God holds reward of both this world and the Hereafter; it prevents reducing goodness to a single material reward. | terra: Whoever wants worldly reward is reminded that both worldly and otherworldly reward are with God, exposing the needless narrowness of choosing only the nearer portion.

luna: The ayah says the bad and good are not equal even if abundance of the bad attracts; this sharpens the source section’s distinction between abundant-looking goods and genuinely good choice. | terra: The foul and the wholesome are not equal even when the foul's abundance impresses, directly correcting a selector who mistakes quantity for good quality.

luna: Worldly life is described as play and amusement, while the Hereafter’s abode is better for those mindful of God; this gives the section’s passing/lasting contrast a direct formulation. | terra: Worldly life is play and diversion, whereas the final abode is better for the God-fearing, stating the same comparative scale.
terra: People deceived by worldly life turn religion into play and diversion; the command to leave them and remind by the Quran ties the bad preference to its reckoning.
terra: مَا قَدَرُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ حَقَّ قَدْرِهِۦ uses the measuring root in the sense of valuing God inadequately, the evaluative sense the section points back to from 87:3.
terra: The weighing on that day is true, and those whose scales are heavy are the successful, literally staging one pan and its selected outcome.
terra: Those whose scales are light have lost themselves through wronging the signs, the discarded side of the same weighing.
terra: Iblis claims أَنَا۠ خَيْرٌ مِّنْهُ on the basis of fire versus clay, showing “better” corrupted into material self-preference.
terra: Worldly adornment and wholesome provision are declared lawful gifts for believers and exclusively theirs at resurrection, preventing “worldly” from being treated as intrinsically refuse.

luna: People are deluded by worldly life and forget the meeting of this day; the root ن س ي named by the source section thus connects discarded remembrance with the consequence of preferring the passing life. | terra: Those deceived by worldly life made religion play; God then says He forgets them as they forgot their meeting, joining the lower choice to treatment as discarded.
terra: God tells Moses that He selected him over the people by His messages and speech, making right preference an informed divine act.
terra: Moses وَٱخْتَارَ مُوسَىٰ قَوْمَهُۥ سَبْعِينَ رَجُلًا, a direct human use of the source dictionary's “choosing” form.

luna: The heirs to scripture seize the lowly, passing goods of this life while expecting forgiveness; this connects the source section’s low-value side to a specific choice of inferior gain over moral fidelity. | terra: Successors repeatedly take عَرَضَ هَٰذَا ٱلْأَدْنَىٰ while the final abode is better for the God-fearing, joining the lower object's root to a recurrent bad selection.
luna: Wealth and children are a trial and a great reward is with God, clarifying that things desired in worldly life test rather than guarantee good.

luna: The ayah says God separates the bad from the good and piles the bad together, a close sorting counterpart to the section’s image of leaving refuse aside. | terra: God separates foul from wholesome, heaps the foul together, and puts it in hell; the rejected material becomes an accumulated refuse pile.
terra: ٱلْعُدْوَةِ ٱلدُّنْيَا means the nearer bank opposite the farther bank, a spatial use that bounds the section's low-value reading of the d-n-w family.

luna: The source section’s verb of preferring is sharpened by this rebuke: the believers sought the immediate spoils, while God willed the Hereafter, making a worldly gain the wrong selection in its context. | terra: تُرِيدُونَ عَرَضَ ٱلدُّنْيَا وَٱللَّهُ يُرِيدُ ٱلْءَاخِرَةَ sets human desire for immediate captive-gain against God's desired horizon.
terra: Captives are told that good known in their hearts can bring them something better than what was taken, placing superior replacement beyond seized property.

luna: The warning names family, wealth, trade, and homes as loves that must not outrank God, His Messenger, and striving; it gives the section’s worldly preference a concrete list and a countermeasure. | terra: Family, acquired wealth, feared commercial loss, and pleasing homes are tested as preferred loves against God, His Messenger, and striving in His way.

luna: The call directly challenges those content with worldly life instead of the Hereafter and calls worldly enjoyment little, closely matching the section’s rebuke of preferring the nearer life. | terra: The question أَرَضِيتُم بِٱلْحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنْيَا مِنَ ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ confronts the addressees' choice and answers that worldly enjoyment is little by comparison.
terra: The unbelievers' word is made the lowest while God's word is the highest, reversing earthly power through an explicit high/low judgment.
terra: The hypocrites forgot God and so He “forgot” them; the reciprocal wording treats willful neglect as exclusion.
luna: God’s purchase of believers’ lives and wealth in exchange for the Garden makes the choice of an enduring reward over worldly possession explicit.

luna: Those who do not expect to meet God are content with worldly life and heedless of the signs; the following ayah names their abode, linking worldly preference with neglected guidance. | terra: Those not expecting the meeting are pleased and settled with worldly life and heedless of the signs, a full description of the wrong preference.

luna: This ayah gives the abode of those described in 10:7 as Fire, completing the consequence of contentment with worldly life alone. | terra: The Fire becomes their shelter because of what they earned, completing the consequence of the settled worldly choice in 10:7.

luna: Rain-fed plants flourish, then become cut stubble as if they had not flourished; this repeats the pasture-to-residue scene behind the section’s contrast of the passing and lasting. | terra: Worldly life is rain-mixed vegetation whose full adornment appears secure just before it is made reaped as though it never flourished.
terra: Their portion is only brief enjoyment in the world, followed by return to God and severe punishment, directly measuring the chosen object against its sequel.

luna: Those who desire worldly life and its adornment receive their deeds’ reward in this life, paralleling the section’s warning about choosing what passes. | terra: Whoever desires worldly life and its adornment receives the full return of deeds there, defining the apparently favored portion before its loss is exposed.

luna: The next ayah completes that worldly bargain: such people have nothing in the Hereafter but Fire, so their immediate reward leaves no enduring share. | terra: The same choosers have only the Fire in the hereafter and their work becomes void, so what looked selected proves to be refuse.
terra: Noah's chiefs label his visibly poor followers أَرَاذِلُنَا; their social sorting mistakes the faithful for human refuse.
terra: Noah refuses to drive away the believers whom the chiefs called lowly in 11:27, so the supposed refuse are retained because they will meet their Lord.
terra: Noah refuses to say that those whom elite eyes despise will receive no good from God, directly overturning the classification of poor believers as refuse.
terra: Shuayb commands full measure and weight with justice and forbids diminishing people's goods, establishing the clean dealing whose divine remainder is better in 11:86.

luna: The source section’s root ب ق ي joins “what remains” to good: in Shuʿayb’s market warning, what God leaves after honest dealing is better for the believers than illicit gain. | terra: بَقِيَّتُ ٱللَّهِ خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ names the lawful remainder left after honest dealing as better, uniting remnant, goodness, and right valuation.

luna: The source section develops ب ق ي as a remnant that still has goodness within it; this ayah calls for people of such a remnant who restrain corruption among earlier peoples. | terra: أُو۟لُوا۟ بَقِيَّةٍ are the remnant with enough moral good to forbid corruption, the exact human sense the section cites.
luna: The ayah says God would not destroy towns while their people are reformers, completing 11:116’s call for a morally sustaining remnant with the consequence its presence can have.
terra: The king says of Joseph, أَسْتَخْلِصْهُ لِنَفْسِى, a concrete act of selecting and reserving someone for oneself like the source dictionary's “setting apart” sense.
terra: After Joseph receives worldly authority, وَلَأَجْرُ ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ خَيْرٌ preserves the section's hierarchy even within a story of justified earthly success.

luna: The source section names the root ء ث ر and this ayah uses its favoring sense: Joseph’s brothers say God preferred him over them, a concrete positive or bestowed preference beside the section’s condemned preference. | terra: Joseph's brothers confess لَقَدْ ءَاثَرَكَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَيْنَا, showing the preference root as God's right elevation of the worthier person.
terra: After asking readers to observe earlier peoples' ends, the ayah says the final abode is better for the God-fearing.

luna: The flood’s foam is carried away while what benefits people remains on earth. This gives the section’s discarded residue and lasting good a vivid parallel, with both a physical remainder and a moral distinction. | terra: Floodwater and molten ore cast up foam that vanishes as refuse, while what benefits people remains on earth; this is the section's sorting of dross from the abiding good in a single image.

luna: Provision may be expanded or restricted, but people rejoice in worldly life although its enjoyment is little beside the Hereafter; abundance alone is not the section’s lasting good. | terra: People rejoice in worldly life although its enjoyment compared with the hereafter is only slight, while the same ayah locates provision under God's measure.
terra: Those who يَسْتَحِبُّونَ ٱلْحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنْيَا عَلَى ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ enact the same preference even with a different verb.
terra: Unbelievers' works are like ashes violently scattered by wind, a specific image of what cannot be retained from the wrong life.
terra: The good word is a good tree with a firm root, beginning a contrast between stable good and uprooted bad.
terra: The good tree continually gives fruit by its Lord's leave, explaining what beneficial persistence looks like.
terra: The bad word is a bad tree uprooted from the earth with no stability, the discarded counterpart to 14:24-25.
terra: The Prophet is told not to extend his eyes toward the enjoyments given to groups of people, a close repeated formulation of 20:131's refusal of worldly display.
terra: Those who answer that their Lord sent good receive good here, but the ayah still declares the final abode better, ordering two genuine goods.
terra: أَرْذَلِ ٱلْعُمُرِ applies “lowest” to extreme old age rather than to a supposedly inferior class of people, a relevant boundary on the refuse metaphor.
terra: The command not to sell God's covenant for a small price says what is with God is better, making a concrete act of the choice whose durability 16:96 explains.

luna: This ayah states the section’s measure of permanence: what people possess runs out, while what is with God remains. | terra: مَا عِندَكُمْ يَنفَدُ وَمَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ بَاقٍ draws the section's exact line between what runs out and what remains.
terra: The righteous believer is promised a good life and a reward according to the best deeds, showing how 16:96's lasting divine store can include rightly ordered present life.
terra: Punishment is traced to their having preferred worldly life over the hereafter, an explicit causal version of the section's rebuke.
terra: A brief enjoyment is followed by painful punishment, compressing the passing lower portion and its enduring cost.

luna: For one who desires the immediate life, God hastens what He wills in it, but the ayah then names Hell as the end; choosing the near reward does not secure lasting good. | terra: Whoever wants the immediate life receives only what God wills and is then assigned hell, directly staging the lower choice and its end.

luna: The paired ayah describes one who desires the Hereafter, strives for it, and believes; the effort is accepted, setting the alternative choice beside the preceding worldly desire. | terra: Whoever wants the hereafter, strives for it, and believes has an appreciated striving, the positive side of 17:18's selection.
terra: God supplies both groups from His bounty, clarifying that the difference lies in what each chooses rather than an unavailable worldly provision.

luna: The ayah notes differences in worldly rank but says the Hereafter has greater degrees and excellence, distinguishing visible worldly status from the fuller scale of value. | terra: Worldly gradations are followed by the declaration that the hereafter is greater in rank and preference, correcting the scale by which people select.
terra: Full measure and straight weighing are called better and best in outcome, joining honest valuation to the comparative good.
terra: Earth's adornment is expressly a test of which people are best in deed, so the attractive surface serves divine selection rather than final value.
terra: God will turn that adorned surface into barren soil, supplying the refuse-like end of what 18:7 made temporarily attractive.

luna: The command not to fix one’s eyes on worldly adornment repeats the scene of 20:131, while its context contrasts patient company with a heedless follower of desire. | terra: The Prophet is commanded to remain with those who call on their Lord and not let his eyes pass beyond them in desire for worldly adornment.
terra: The wealthy man enters his garden wronging himself and declares that it will never perish, explicitly mistaking attractive property for permanence.
terra: He doubts the Hour yet expects an even better return if restored to his Lord, showing the wrong chooser also misappropriating the word “better.”
terra: His produce is encompassed and he wrings his hands over what he spent while the garden lies collapsed, turning the selected display into waste.
terra: After the rich man's garden is ruined, true protection belongs to God and He is better in reward and outcome; the collapsed worldly selection leads into 18:45-46's general likeness.

luna: A rain-fed growth cycle ends with dry fragments scattered by the wind, closely staging the section’s pasture becoming worthless residue and the disappearance of worldly display. | terra: The likeness of worldly life becomes rain-grown vegetation and then wind-scattered stubble, joining the lower life directly to the pasture's discarded residue.

luna: The ayah calls wealth and children the adornment of worldly life, then says enduring righteous deeds are better in reward and hope; this is the section’s transient adornment versus lasting good in direct terms. | terra: After naming wealth and children as worldly adornment, the ayah calls ٱلْبَٰقِيَٰتُ ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتُ better with the Lord, the good remainder opposite 18:45's stubble.
luna: Those who turn away from God’s signs forget what their own hands have sent ahead; this makes the section’s forgetting image an act of neglect whose consequences remain.
terra: The question about those greatest in loss introduces a sorting whose rejected side does not recognize itself.
terra: Their striving is lost in worldly life while they think they are doing well, exactly portraying refuse mistakenly selected as good work.
terra: Mary's wish to have been نَسْيًا مَّنسِيًّا uses the root for a forgotten, discarded thing, exactly the section's secondary refuse sense.
terra: وَمَا كَانَ رَبُّكَ نَسِيًّا excludes forgetfulness from the Lord, bounding the discarded-object sense attached to created beings.

luna: The source section’s root ب ق ي is given moral content as lasting righteous deeds, which are better with the Lord in reward and outcome. | terra: وَٱلْبَٰقِيَٰتُ ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتُ خَيْرٌ repeats the union of remaining good and superior value, while God increases the guided in guidance.
terra: وَأَنَا ٱخْتَرْتُكَ addresses Moses with the very اختيار form whose dictionary sense the section explains.
terra: وَٱصْطَنَعْتُكَ لِنَفْسِى addresses Moses as one formed and set apart for God, a nonlexical enactment of reserving a chosen person to oneself.

luna: Moses says his Lord neither errs nor forgets and that knowledge is in a record; this is a specific counter-image to forgetting, though the ayah speaks of divine knowledge rather than the Prophet’s recitation. | terra: Moses says his Lord neither errs nor forgets, distinguishing divine preservation of the record from human forgetting and abandonment.

luna: The source section’s root ء ث ر is voiced here as the magicians refuse to prefer Pharaoh over the clear signs and their Creator; his power reaches only this worldly life, making their choice under threat a pointed counterpart to preferring it. | terra: The threatened magicians say لَن نُّؤْثِرَكَ over the proofs and their Creator, reversing 87:16's censured preference while limiting Pharaoh's power to this worldly life.

luna: This is the source section’s exact pairing of خير and أبقى: the magicians end by naming God better and more enduring, after refusing Pharaoh’s worldly authority. | terra: The magicians conclude وَٱللَّهُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ; the exact better-and-more-lasting pair names what their refusal in 20:72 selects.

luna: The same Taha narrative says the criminal does not die or live in Hell, recalling the section’s image of suspended existence and bounding its promise of a lasting good with a lasting punishment. | terra: Immediately after the magicians choose God as better and more lasting, the criminal's hell is described as a state of neither dying nor living, showing the dreadful side of continued existence.
luna: Whoever turns away from God’s remembrance is promised a constricted life and blindness at resurrection, a specific consequence for choosing heedlessness over reminder.
luna: The person asks why he is raised blind though he once saw, introducing the next ayah’s link between neglect and being forgotten.

luna: The answer says the person forgot God’s signs and is forgotten today; this completes the reversal between what was neglected and what remains at judgment. | terra: The person who forgot God's signs is told وَكَذَٰلِكَ ٱلْيَوْمَ تُنسَىٰ, turning chosen neglect into being left forgotten before 20:127 names the more enduring punishment.

luna: The source section explicitly notes the contrary use of أبقى: here the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more lasting, so permanence itself does not make an outcome good. | terra: The punishment of the hereafter is أَشَدُّ وَأَبْقَىٰ; it is a direct boundary on treating persistence itself as proof of goodness.

luna: The source section’s two sides meet in one address: do not fix one’s eyes on the worldly life’s flower; the Lord’s provision is better and more enduring. | terra: The worldly display is a flower not to be stared at, while وَرِزْقُ رَبِّكَ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ joins the pasture image to better, lasting provision.
terra: The command to persist in prayer and the assurance “We provide for you” give the lived discipline behind 20:131's choice of the Lord's better provision.
terra: A destroyed town's people become حَصِيدًا خَٰمِدِينَ, “mown down and extinguished,” a nonlexical parallel to humans made field refuse.
terra: The same phrase أَرْذَلِ ٱلْعُمُرِ describes senescence in a resurrection argument, preserving the low-value word while changing its object and moral force.
terra: The repeated formula that people did not value God at His true value connects measurement-language to failed spiritual appraisal.
terra: God selects messengers from angels and humans, another explicit selection whose criterion belongs to the all-hearing, all-seeing chooser.

luna: The deniers reduce existence to worldly life, death, and living again without resurrection; their denial of any enduring Hereafter is a sharp contrary boundary to the section’s preference for what lasts.

luna: The source section’s root غ ث و appears for people struck down and made into refuse; here the debris image extends from withered growth to a destroyed people and warns against rejecting the messengers. | terra: After the blast seizes the wrongdoers, God makes them غُثَآءً; people themselves become the pasture refuse invoked by the section's dictionary sense.
luna: The question asks whether abundant wealth and children mean that good things are being hastened to people; it challenges the equation of worldly abundance with true good.
luna: This ayah answers that such people do not perceive that the abundance may be a trial, completing the challenge to treat material plenty as the selected good.
terra: Heavy scales identify the successful, repeating the selection-by-weight that the section evokes with its two pans.
terra: Light scales identify those who lose themselves and remain in hell, completing the opposed result.

luna: Believers are described as people whom trade and sale do not distract from remembering God, prayer, and giving; this is the opposite ordering to the section’s preference for worldly life. | terra: People whom neither commerce nor sale distracts from remembrance and prayer embody the opposite of the crowd that chose commerce in 62:11.
terra: Rejecters' deeds are like a desert mirage that the thirsty person takes for water but finds to be nothing, a specific false selection by appearance.
terra: God turns the unbelievers' apparent works into scattered dust, a direct image of selected-looking deeds proving to be refuse.
terra: Noah is challenged for having ٱلْأَرْذَلُونَ as followers, staging the elite's false identification of low status with low worth.
terra: Noah answers the charge about lowly followers by denying knowledge of their deeds, refusing the chiefs' superficial basis for sorting them.
terra: Their account belongs only to the Lord, relocating judgment of the supposed human refuse to the one who knows their worth.
terra: وَمَآ أَنَا۠ بِطَارِدِ ٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ is Noah's refusal to discard the followers labeled “the lowest” in 26:111.
terra: The people build monumental structures as though they might live forever, another explicit attempt to extract permanence from worldly possession.
terra: Solomon rejects the envoys' gift because what God has given him is better than what they offer; their delight in the gift reveals the lesser valuation.
terra: Many settlements exulting in their livelihood are destroyed, leaving dwellings scarcely inhabited and inherited by God; plentiful provision becomes abandoned remainder.

luna: What people are given is described as enjoyment and adornment of worldly life, while what is with God is better and more lasting, the section’s distinction applied to possessions. | terra: Worldly gifts are temporary enjoyment and adornment, whereas وَمَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ states the section's valuation exactly.
terra: A person who meets God's good promise is contrasted with one merely given worldly enjoyment and then brought for judgment, continuing 28:60's comparison as two human outcomes.

luna: The source section defines choosing as seeking and doing what is better; this ayah says God creates and chooses, shifting the act of choosing to the Creator and bounding human preference. | terra: وَرَبُّكَ يَخْلُقُ مَا يَشَآءُ وَيَخْتَارُ reserves creation and choosing to the Lord and denies creatures an independent right of selection.
terra: Qarun's immense treasure and oppressive conduct establish the abundance whose value 28:77-82 subsequently overturns.

luna: The command to seek the Hereafter with what God has given while not forgetting one’s share of worldly life supplies a boundary: preferring the lasting good need not mean erasing ordinary worldly provision. | terra: Qarun is told to seek the final home with his gifts without forgetting his legitimate worldly share, a boundary on construing right preference as rejecting every present good.
terra: Qarun attributes his wealth to his own knowledge, claiming a corrupt source of merit for the property others will desire in 28:79.
terra: Those desiring worldly life see Qarun's splendor and wish for his portion, a narrated instance of selecting by the lower life's glitter.
terra: People given knowledge answer that God's reward is better for the believer who acts rightly, correcting the spectators' standard of choice.
terra: Qarun and his house are swallowed by the earth, making the coveted display in 28:79 into discarded ruin.
terra: Those who had desired Qarun's place now recognize God's control of provision and that unbelievers do not prosper, narrating the correction of their choice.
terra: The final home is assigned to those who do not seek elevation or corruption on earth, reversing the instinct to choose worldly height.

luna: The ayah says all things perish except His Face and that all return to Him, a direct formulation of the permanence singled out by the source section’s root ء ث ر branch about remaining alone. | terra: كُلُّ شَىْءٍ هَالِكٌ إِلَّا وَجْهَهُۥ gives the absolute boundary between everything perishing and God alone remaining.

luna: This ayah calls worldly life play and amusement and the Hereafter the true life, making the section’s contrast between temporary and enduring life explicit. | terra: Worldly life is play and diversion, while the final abode is called the true life; the ayah reverses the surface judgment of what deserves choosing.
terra: أَدْنَى ٱلْأَرْضِ locates the Romans' defeat in the nearer land, preserving the root's spatial sense rather than a judgment of baseness.
luna: People know only the outward aspect of worldly life and are heedless of the Hereafter; this names the narrowed valuation that the section challenges.

luna: An increase sought through usury does not increase with God, while charity seeking God’s face is multiplied; this distinguishes apparent material gain from value that endures. | terra: Usury given to increase through people's wealth does not increase with God, while alms seeking God's face are the true multipliers.
terra: The repeated command not to let worldly life deceive warns that present appearance can corrupt the choice made for the coming day.

luna: The people in punishment are told they forgot the meeting of this day and are now abandoned to it; what was treated as forgettable has persisted as their outcome. | terra: The condemned are told that, because they forgot the meeting of their day, they too are forgotten and made to taste lasting punishment.
terra: The Prophet's wives are offered a literal choice: worldly life and adornment with an honorable release.
terra: Choosing God, His Messenger, and the final home instead brings the good-doers a great reward, completing the two-sided offer of 33:28.
terra: People infer immunity from punishment from greater wealth and children, making abundance their false proof of chosen status.
terra: God expands and restricts provision, but most people do not know; possession therefore cannot bear the value assigned to it in 34:35.
terra: Neither wealth nor children bring people near to God; faith and right action instead receive multiplied reward and secure chambers.
terra: God's promise is true, so worldly life must not deceive; the same formula directly pits deceptive nearness against promised reality.
terra: Those selected to inherit the Book still include a self-wronging group, a moderate boundary on the dictionary ideal that what is chosen contains no low element.
terra: God records what people send ahead and the آثار they leave behind, giving the preference root's “traces” family a concrete relation to what remains.
terra: ٱلسَّمَآءَ ٱلدُّنْيَا is the nearest heaven adorned with stars, a repeated nonmoral use of the same adjective as worldly life.
terra: After the flood, Noah's descendants are made the surviving remainder, a human remnant preserved from a destroyed world.

terra: Solomon's حُبَّ ٱلْخَيْرِ concerns prized horses and remembrance of his Lord; it plausibly exemplifies “good” as valuable property, though the precise relation between that love and remembrance is interpretively disputed.
terra: وَإِنَّهُمْ عِندَنَا لَمِنَ ٱلْمُصْطَفَيْنَ ٱلْأَخْيَارِ brings “selected” and “the best” together, matching the section's claim that selection seeks good.
terra: Iblis again calls himself better than Adam from their materials, a repeated warning that comparative “good” can voice arrogant misvaluation.
terra: Those who listen to speech and follow its best are the divinely guided, presenting right selection as discerning and doing the better option.

luna: Crops grow in varied colors, yellow, then become debris; this is another direct growth-to-waste scene that makes the section’s discarded residue concrete. | terra: Rain-grown crops vary, yellow, and become debris; the sequence reproduces pasture becoming discard and is offered as a reminder to discerning minds.
terra: The command to follow the best of what the Lord has sent down makes discernment of the best an urgent act before punishment arrives.
terra: Failure to value God truly is answered by the earth in His grasp and the heavens folded in His hand, exposing the small scale behind worldly misvaluation.

luna: The speaker calls worldly life only a temporary enjoyment and the Hereafter the lasting home, directly articulating the section’s value distinction. | terra: This life is called temporary enjoyment while the hereafter is دَارُ ٱلْقَرَارِ, the settled abode, directly opposing passing possession to permanence.
terra: The nearest heaven is adorned with lamps, confirming that dunyā can mark proximity without calling its noun morally low.

luna: The ayah contrasts the one who seeks the Hereafter’s harvest and has it increased with the one who seeks the world’s harvest and receives only some of it; the harvest image joins the pasture scene to the choice of what lasts. | terra: The cultivator of the hereafter has that harvest increased, while the cultivator of the world gets some of it but no otherworldly share; the agricultural image makes selection yield its own crop.

luna: The ayah explicitly calls worldly provision enjoyment, then says what is with God is better and lasting for believers; it closely matches the section’s two sides. | terra: Worldly gifts are enjoyment of this life, while وَمَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ identifies the believers' better, enduring share.
terra: Abraham makes the declaration a remaining word among his descendants, an enduring good residue meant to bring later people back.

luna: The ayah describes God distributing worldly livelihoods and ranks, then says the Lord’s mercy is better than what people accumulate, distinguishing provision from the greater good. | terra: God apportions worldly livelihood and raises people in degrees, yet His mercy is better than what they collect, relocating value beyond social rank and accumulation.

luna: The ayah says worldly adornment is only enjoyment of this life and that the Hereafter belongs to the mindful, connecting material display to the section’s temporary side. | terra: Silver and gold adornment are declared no more than worldly enjoyment, while the hereafter with the Lord belongs to the God-fearing.
terra: Pharaoh asks whether he is better than “this contemptible one,” turning worldly kingship and abasement into the very false scale the section corrects.
terra: وَلَقَدِ ٱخْتَرْنَٰهُمْ عَلَىٰ عِلْمٍ states God's knowledgeable selection of a people over the worlds, a direct use of the dictionary form.
luna: Those who claim only worldly life and death are corrected by the reminder that time does not erase accountability; this reverses the preference’s assumption that nothing remains.

luna: The people are told they forgot the meeting of this day and are now forgotten, with Fire as their abode; this links worldly delusion to an afterlife consequence that cannot be discarded. | terra: إِنَّا نَسِينَٰكُمْ كَمَا نَسِيتُمْ لِقَآءَ يَوْمِكُمْ makes reciprocal forgetting the fate of those who discarded the encounter.
terra: The reason given is that they mocked the signs and worldly life deceived them, explicitly linking 45:34's abandonment to the wrong-valued life.

luna: On the Day of Judgment, the disbelievers are told they used up their good things in worldly life and enjoyed them; this makes the temporary enjoyment’s later cost explicit. | terra: The Fire's people are told they exhausted their good things in worldly life and enjoyed them there, so their chosen portion leaves humiliation for the present day.

luna: This ayah calls worldly life play and diversion, then links belief and mindfulness to reward; it names the passing side and the choice that points beyond it. | terra: Worldly life is play and diversion, while faith and reverence preserve the promised rewards rather than consuming people's wealth.

luna: The Prophet is told to turn from one who turns away from remembrance and wants only worldly life, directly joining the section’s preference for the world to avoidance of reminder. | terra: The command turns away from one who turns from remembrance and desires only worldly life, joining exclusive lower desire to rejected guidance.

luna: The neighboring ayah says the worldly desirer’s knowledge reaches only that limit, completing the preceding warning about turning from remembrance for worldly life. | terra: ذَٰلِكَ مَبْلَغُهُم مِّنَ ٱلْعِلْمِ identifies desire for only worldly life in 53:29 as the limit of their knowledge and contrasts it with God's knowledge of guidance.
terra: وَثَمُودَا۟ فَمَآ أَبْقَىٰ states that no one of Thamud was left, contrasting moral remnant with annihilated residue.

luna: Everything on earth is passing away, the temporal side of the section’s distinction; the next ayah names what remains. | terra: كُلُّ مَنْ عَلَيْهَا فَانٍ states the passing side of the section's division without metaphorical extension.

luna: The next ayah says the face of the Lord of majesty and honor remains, completing the preceding claim and giving the source section’s “God alone in permanence” idea a Qur’anic formulation. | terra: وَيَبْقَىٰ وَجْهُ رَبِّكَ gives the surviving side and supports the dictionary claim that God alone possesses unconditioned permanence.
terra: فِيهِنَّ خَيْرَٰتٌ حِسَانٌ is the Quranic form illuminated by the source dictionary gloss “chosen women, with no base one among them.”

luna: The ayah compares worldly life to rain-fed growth that pleases, yellows, and becomes debris, while warning that the world’s adornment and rivalry are only temporary enjoyment. | terra: Worldly life is compared to rain-grown plants that yellow and become debris before the ayah sets punishment, forgiveness, and divine approval beyond them.
terra: After worldly vegetation becomes debris in 57:20, the command to race toward forgiveness and a vast garden identifies what should be actively selected.
luna: This preceding ayah identifies the emigrants who were driven from their homes and seek God’s bounty; it completes the setting for the Anṣār’s preference in 59:9.

luna: The source section explicitly links ء ث ر to favoring another over oneself: the Anṣār put the emigrants first even when needy, and the ayah calls these people successful, showing preference directed toward good. | terra: The Helpers يُؤْثِرُونَ عَلَىٰٓ أَنفُسِهِمْ despite need, enacting the dictionary's good sense of preferring another and ending in success.

luna: Those who forget God are made to forget themselves; this gives the section’s root ن س ي a moral reversal in which neglect of what matters destroys one’s own orientation. | terra: Those who forget God are made to forget themselves, sharpening the section's notion that what one discards in choice can turn the chooser into the discarded.
luna: Before the market scene in the following ayah, the Friday call commands people to leave trade and hasten to God’s remembrance; the command makes the choice staged in 62:11 legible.
luna: After prayer, people are permitted to disperse and seek God’s bounty; this completes the market passage and bounds its rebuke as a matter of priority, not a ban on livelihood.

luna: When trade or amusement appears, people leave the Messenger standing; the ayah says what is with God is better than trade and amusement, a precise scene of choosing immediate display over a better provision. | terra: People leave the Messenger standing when they see commerce or amusement, and the ayah answers that what is with God is better than both and that He is the best provider.

luna: Believers are warned not to let wealth and children distract them from remembering God; those who do so are the losers, a specific account of the section’s condemned preference. | terra: The believers are commanded not to let wealth or children distract them from remembrance; those who do are named the losers.
luna: Wealth and children are called a trial, while a great reward is with God; the ayah clarifies why worldly goods cannot stand in for the good that remains.
terra: The nearest heaven is adorned with lamps, another exact boundary on deriving moral worth from the adjective alone.
terra: The owners of the garden are made a test when they swear to harvest it in the morning, beginning a scene in which ownership and selection are morally exposed.
terra: They make no exception for God's will, marking the self-enclosed claim beneath their confidence in the crop.
terra: The garden becomes like a dark, harvested field overnight, turning the expected choice produce into unusable residue.
terra: The owners whisper that no poor person is to enter the garden, revealing that their intended harvest excludes rather than selflessly prefers the needy.
terra: They go out convinced of their power to withhold, the wrong preference immediately before discovering the field's ruin.
terra: On seeing the garden they first think they have lost the way, because the selected property is no longer recognizable.
terra: They then confess that they are deprived, reversing their plan to deprive the poor.
terra: They hope their Lord will replace the garden with one better than it, turning loss into a newly corrected request for the better portion.
terra: The passage concludes that worldly punishment is like this but the punishment of the hereafter is greater, measuring the ruined crop against the lasting consequence.
terra: فَهَلْ تَرَىٰ لَهُم مِّنۢ بَاقِيَةٍ asks whether any remnant of the destroyed people can be seen, the negative edge of the section's valuable remainder.
terra: Whatever good people send ahead for themselves will be found with God as something better and greater in reward.
luna: The passage addresses the Prophet’s tongue as he hastens to recite revelation, repeating the recitation setting of the source section’s assurance that he will not forget.
luna: This ayah says God takes responsibility for gathering and reciting the revelation, directly paralleling the source section’s promise of recitation and preservation.
luna: The next ayah instructs the Prophet to follow the recitation when it is recited, completing the same revelation scene.
luna: The final ayah in this sequence assigns the explanation of the recitation to God, completing the passage that parallels the source section’s recitation and not-forgetting.

luna: The ayah says people love the immediate life, an especially concise statement of the preference condemned by the source section. | terra: كَلَّا بَلْ تُحِبُّونَ ٱلْعَاجِلَةَ rebukes the same collective attachment as 87:16, calling its object the immediate life.

luna: The next ayah says they leave the Hereafter, completing the immediate-life preference as an explicit two-sided choice. | terra: وَتَذَرُونَ ٱلْءَاخِرَةَ makes explicit that loving the immediate means leaving the lasting counterpart unchosen.

luna: The righteous feed the needy, orphan, and captive despite their love of the food, a concrete enactment of preferring others over oneself. | terra: Feeding the needy, orphan, and captive despite love for the food plausibly enacts preferring others over self, though عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِۦ can also be read as love of God.
luna: The next ayah says they seek neither repayment nor thanks, completing the selfless giving scene with its orientation toward God rather than worldly return.
terra: إِنَّ هَٰؤُلَآءِ يُحِبُّونَ ٱلْعَاجِلَةَ وَيَذَرُونَ وَرَآءَهُمْ يَوْمًا ثَقِيلًا restages choosing the near life and casting the consequential day behind.

luna: The source section’s warning about preferring the lowly worldly life is stated directly: this person “preferred the life of this world,” and the following ayah gives the destination. | terra: وَءَاثَرَ ٱلْحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنْيَا is the section's wrong preference verb and object repeated exactly in the Pharaoh passage.

luna: The following ayah completes the worldly preference’s outcome by naming Hell as its abode, the negative side of the section’s choice between transient and enduring outcomes. | terra: Hell becoming the wrong chooser's shelter supplies the consequence of 79:38 and one side of the section's openly staged selection.

luna: The other side of the passage is the one who fears standing before the Lord and restrains the self from desire, matching the section’s account of choosing the better rather than the lower impulse. | terra: Fear of standing before the Lord and restraining the self from desire enact the opposite choice to preferring the lower life.

luna: This ayah completes the other side of the choice: the Garden is the abode of the one who feared and restrained desire. | terra: Paradise becoming the shelter completes 79:40 and the two-outcome sorting begun by 79:38-39.
terra: A person reads abundant provision as divine honor, showing the worldly valuation the following ayat reject.
terra: Restricted provision is read as humiliation, the matching error of confusing measured wealth with human worth.
terra: كَلَّا rejects both readings and redirects value toward honoring the orphan.

luna: The source section develops wealth as part of the worldly side; this ayah says people love wealth intensely, making that material pull concrete, though it does not use the source section’s root خ ي ر. | terra: وَتُحِبُّونَ ٱلْمَالَ حُبًّا جَمًّا names the excessive love that makes wealth occupy the favored pan.
luna: The successful person is the one who purifies the soul, a specific inner counterpart to the section’s claim that the right choice selects what is good rather than refuse.
luna: The neighboring ayah gives the opposite outcome to the one who buries the soul, completing the passage’s purification-versus-loss contrast.
luna: The person who gives and is mindful of God receives the promised easy path, beginning a passage where generosity rather than self-protective holding directs one’s choice.
luna: Belief in the best promise completes the giver’s orientation in the preceding ayah, a choice directed toward an outcome beyond immediate possession.
luna: The next ayah says God will ease this person toward ease, completing the positive consequence of giving and belief.
luna: The passage’s opposite person is miserly, self-sufficient, and denying the best promise; that reversal makes the choice in the section concrete.
luna: The next ayah completes the negative orientation as denial of the best promise, rather than merely having little wealth.
luna: The miser is eased toward hardship, completing the two-sided outcome of the choices contrasted in 92:5–9.

luna: The following ayah says the person’s wealth will not avail him when he falls, completing the passage’s distinction between possessions and lasting outcome. | terra: The question of what wealth can avail when its owner falls denies accumulated property any power to preserve him.

luna: The Prophet is assured that the Hereafter is better for him than the first life, a concise formulation of the section’s valuation spoken as reassurance. | terra: وَلَلْءَاخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ لَّكَ مِنَ ٱلْأُولَىٰ gives the Prophet the same better-later valuation in a personal promise.
terra: Humanity is created فِىٓ أَحْسَنِ تَقْوِيمٍ, establishing the high-value starting point of the following sorting.

luna: After being created in the best form, the human can be brought low; this parallels the section’s contrast between high value and the lowly side of worldly preference, though the surah’s focus is human moral condition. | terra: ثُمَّ رَدَدْنَٰهُ أَسْفَلَ سَٰفِلِينَ supplies the lowest side of the high/low human valuation, before 95:6 preserves the faithful exception.
terra: Believers who do right are excepted from the fall to the lowest and receive an unfailing reward, joining goodness to an undiminished remainder.
terra: Persistent rejecters are called the worst of creatures and assigned hell, supplying the rejected human side of an explicit best/worst sorting.
terra: Believers who act rightly are called the best of creatures, the selected side opposite 98:6.
terra: The best creatures receive gardens خَٰلِدِينَ فِيهَآ أَبَدًا, joining their goodness to enduring reward.

luna: The source section’s root خ ي ر also appears here in the sense of wealth: intense love of material good can pull a person toward the worldly side the section warns about. | terra: وَإِنَّهُۥ لِحُبِّ ٱلْخَيْرِ لَشَدِيدٌ uses ٱلْخَيْر for wealth and makes intense attachment to it part of the human misvaluation.

luna: The heavy scales mark the person whose good deeds outweigh, a concrete sorting of outcomes that parallels the section’s selection of what has true value. | terra: A person with heavy scales begins the surah's compact two-pan sorting.
luna: The next ayah names that person’s pleasant life, completing the positive outcome of the heavy scales. | terra: A pleasing life is the result assigned to the heavy scales.

luna: The ayah turns to the person whose scales are light, the contrary side of the sorting that the section imagines as leaving refuse behind. | terra: Light scales introduce the rejected side of the same valuation.

luna: The next ayah uses the term commonly rendered as “the abyss” for the light-scaled person, completing the consequence of the negative measure. | terra: The abyss becomes the light-scaled person's home, completing the choice's terminal contrast.

luna: Rivalry in piling up possessions distracts people, a concrete form of choosing worldly accumulation over remembrance of what endures. | terra: Rivalry in accumulation distracts people, a compressed account of abundance becoming the wrongly preferred measure.

luna: The next ayah says the rivalry lasts until visiting the graves, completing the accumulation scene with death as its limit. | terra: The distraction persists until people visit the graves, exposing the temporal limit hidden by accumulation.

luna: The person who gathers and counts wealth supplies a concrete instance of worldly possession treated as the desired good. | terra: The condemned person gathers and repeatedly counts wealth, a concrete attachment to the supposedly chosen worldly portion.

luna: The next ayah says the wealth collector thinks his wealth will make him last forever, a direct reversal of the source section’s distinction between passing wealth and true permanence. | terra: يَحْسَبُ أَنَّ مَالَهُۥٓ أَخْلَدَهُ exposes the mistake of treating accumulated wealth as a source of permanence.
terra: The army is made like eaten straw, another concrete reversal in which the apparently powerful become agricultural residue.
